stories.headline: Seattle Times and Newsday sue OpenAI and Microsoft for copyright infringement
stories.hook: Two major publishers join the fray, naming Microsoft as a co-defendant alongside OpenAI.
stories.tldr: The Seattle Times and Newsday have filed lawsuits against OpenAI and Microsoft, alleging copyright infringement. The suit targets OpenAI’s training practices and names Microsoft as a defendant because its Copilot product is built on OpenAI technology. This legal action mirrors similar suits brought by The New York Times, Ziff Davis, Merriam-Webster, and Encyclopedia Britannica. The filings represent an escalation in the ongoing conflict between legacy media and generative AI developers over the use of copyrighted content without compensation or consent.

body.text: The Seattle Times and Newsday have joined the growing list of plaintiffs taking OpenAI to court, alleging copyright infringement. This is not an isolated incident but part of a broader pattern involving The New York Times, Ziff Davis, Merriam-Webster, and Encyclopedia Britannica. What distinguishes this filing is the inclusion of Microsoft as a co-defendant. The publishers argue that Microsoft should be held accountable because its Copilot product is built directly on OpenAI’s technology. By naming both entities, the lawsuit attempts to pierce the corporate veil that often separates model development from distribution. It forces a conversation about who benefits from the extraction of copyrighted text and who holds the legal responsibility for it. The fine print of these agreements usually favors the platform, but this suit challenges that assumption by linking the output directly to the infrastructure provider.

You are seeing the architecture of liability shift in real time. Previously, the argument was always about the training data itself. Now, it is about the commercial application. Microsoft cannot claim innocence when Copilot is the primary vehicle delivering OpenAI's outputs to users. This creates a direct line of sight between the revenue-generating product and the alleged infringement. It unlocks a new phase where distributors must audit their underlying models more rigorously. The steep curve here is that tech giants can no longer outsource their legal risks to their API providers. They own the user experience, so they own the risk. This changes how every B2B AI deal is structured going forward.

The receipt here is simple: if you profit from the work, you pay for the rights. The lawsuit does not ask for vague promises of better ethics committees or voluntary opt-out buttons. It demands accountability through the legal system. The involvement of Microsoft is particularly significant because it ties the legal fate of the AI division to the broader corporate entity. This ensures that any settlement or judgment has teeth. It prevents the company from simply absorbing the cost as a business expense while continuing the same practices. The publishers are effectively saying that the current model of scraping the web for free is legally unsustainable. They are betting that the courts will agree that copyright law still applies to machine learning pipelines.
